# 1. Introduction and data cleaning

Multinomial regression contributes three things other methods cannot:

1.  Directly interpretable coefficients. Each coefficient is a log-odds ratio for one outcome relative to a baseline (the match being a draw in our case).

2.  It directly estimates probabilities for Home, Draw and Away. This simplifies the computation of performance metrics and helps with classification.

3.  It provides a benchmark for assessing whether more complex methods are worth it e.g. if random forests or SVMs perform similarly, their added complexity may offer little benefit.

## 1.2 Load the data and define the outcome

```{r}

train_raw <- read.csv("~/GitHub/Sprint-1/processed-data/football_train_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

test_raw <- read.csv("~/GitHub/Sprint-1/processed-data/football_test_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# HS = Home shots, AS = Away shots, HST = Home shots on target, AST = Away shots on target, HF = Home fouls, AF = Away fouls, HC = Home corners, AC = Away corners, HY = Home yellow cards, AY = Away yellow cards, HR = Home red cards, AR = Away red cards. 
stats_all <- c(
  "HS", "AS", "HST", "AST", "HF", "AF",
  "HC", "AC", "HY", "AY", "HR", "AR"
)

# Bookmaker odds
odds_cols <- c("B365H", "B365D", "B365A")
# H = home win, D = draw, A = away win.
outcome_levels <- c("D", "A", "H")
```

## 1.3 Clean the rows and create simple features

We remove rows with missing outcomes or missing values in the 12 match statistics. This keeps model comparisons on the same matches. It may introduce bias if missingness is related to the match or league.

We also create differences (home minus away) and totals (home plus away). The difference describes which side has the advantage and the total describes the overall output during the match.

```{r}

prepare_matches <- function(data, predictors) {
  
  keep <- complete.cases(data[, c("FTR", predictors), drop = FALSE])
  data <- data[keep, , drop = FALSE]

  # Differences
  data$d_sot <- data$HST - data$AST
  data$d_shots <- data$HS - data$AS
  data$d_corners <- data$HC - data$AC

  # Totals
  data$t_sot <- data$HST + data$AST
  data$t_shots <- data$HS + data$AS
  data$t_corners <- data$HC + data$AC

  data
}

# Main data
train_main <- prepare_matches(train_raw, stats_all)
test_main <- prepare_matches(test_raw, stats_all)

cat("Training rows in original file:", nrow(train_raw), "\n")
cat("Training rows used:", nrow(train_main), "\n")
cat("Premier League test rows in original file:", nrow(test_raw), "\n")
cat("Premier League test rows used:", nrow(test_main), "\n")
```

# 2. Initial EDA

## 2.1 Compare the outcome balance

Home wins are the most common outcome in both the training and test data sets, with slightly more home wins in the Premier League sample. If we always predict a Home win this achieves $45.49\%$ test accuracy, providing a more meaningful baseline than $1/3$ accuracy.

```{r}
class_share <- rbind(
  `Lower league - training` = prop.table(table(factor(train_main$FTR, levels = outcome_levels))),
  `Premier League - test` = prop.table(table(factor(test_main$FTR, levels = outcome_levels)))
)

colnames(class_share) <- c("Draw", "Away win", "Home win")

barplot(
  t(class_share), beside = TRUE,
  names.arg = rownames(class_share),
  legend.text = colnames(class_share),
  ylab = "Proportion of matches",
  main = "Outcome balance in training and test data",
  ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1
)
```

```{r, fig.height=7}
idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(train_main)), min(1500, nrow(train_main)))
pairs(train_main[idx, c("HS", "AS", "HST", "AST", "HC", "AC")],
      pch = 16, cex = 0.35, main = "Relationships between attacking statistics (sample)")
round(cor(train_main[, stats_all]), 2)
```

## 2.2 Check for redundancy

Shots and shots on target are moderately correlated for both home and away teams $(r=0.62, r=0.63)$. This suggests overlapping information and motivates comparing the full model with smaller alternatives.

```{r, fig.height=7}
correlation_matrix <- cor(train_main[, stats_all])
corrplot(correlation_matrix, method = "color", addCoef.col = "black")
```

## 2.3 Look at the relationship between shot advantage and result

This plot groups matches by the difference between home and away shots on target. It shows whether home wins become more common as the home side's advantage increases.

```{r}
# Use quantiles to make groups 
cut_points <- unique(quantile(train_main$d_sot,probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),))

shot_group <- cut(train_main$d_sot, breaks = cut_points, include.lowest = TRUE)
shot_group <- droplevels(shot_group)

result_by_shot_group <- prop.table(table(shot_group, factor(train_main$FTR, levels = outcome_levels)),margin = 1)

barplot(
  t(result_by_shot_group), beside = TRUE,
  names.arg = rownames(result_by_shot_group),
   legend.text = c("Draw", "Away win", "Home win"),
   ylab = "Observed proportion",
   main = "Observed result by home-minus-away shots on target",
   las = 2, cex.names = 0.7, ylim = c(0, 1)
)
```

We look at outcome proportions across shots on target differences to investigate how a relative attacking advantage relates to results. This motivates a difference based predictor and a sensitivity analysis excluding shots on target to see if we gain information by including it.

# 3. Model selection

## 3.1 What multinomial logistic regression estimates

The response has three unordered classes: draw, away win and home win. Multinomial logistic regression estimates a probability for each class, with the probabilities adding to one:

$$
P(Y_i = k \mid \mathbf{x}_i) =
\frac{\exp(\alpha_k + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_k)}
{\sum_{j \in \{D,A,H\}} \exp(\alpha_j + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_j)}.
$$

This model estimates probabilities for Home, Draw and Away. With Draw as the reference, coefficients describe changes in home versus draw and away versus draw log-odds.

## 3.2 Models to compare

Each model addresses a specific question, whether shots on target dominate performance, whether other statistics add information, and whether an interaction term improves fit. Backward selection tests whether a smaller model is sufficient.

1.  **Null baseline:** intercept only
2.  **Full statistics:** includes all 12 statistics
3.  **Shots and corners:** a smaller model focused on attacking output
4.  **Differences and totals:** differenced and total statistics between home and away
5.  **Difference total interaction:** interaction term
6.  **Without shots on target:** checks whether the result depends heavily on SoT.
7.  **Backward AIC:** starts with the full model and removes terms when it improves AIC.

Why I've chosen to investigate the interaction term ? A difference of two shots on target could mean 4 versus 2 or 12 versus 10. The difference is the same, but the overall match output is not. The interaction tests whether the relationship between the difference and outcome changes with the total and if it can accurately classify our matches.

```{r}
# Models I'd like to try.
formulas_main <- list(
  "Null baseline" = FTR ~ 1,
  
  "Only Shots on target" = FTR ~ HST + AST,

  "Full statistics" = FTR ~ HS + AS + HST + AST + HF + AF +
    HC + AC + HY + AY + HR + AR,

  "Shots and corners" = FTR ~ HST + AST + HS + AS + HC + AC,

  "Differences and totals" = FTR ~ d_sot + t_sot +
    d_shots + t_shots + d_corners + t_corners,

  "Difference total interaction" = FTR ~ d_sot * t_sot +
    d_shots + t_shots + d_corners + t_corners,

  "Without shots on target" = FTR ~ HS + AS + HF + AF +
    HC + AC + HY + AY + HR + AR
)

# Model names
main_model_names <- c(names(formulas_main), "Backward AIC")

main_fits <- list()

# Fit 
for (model_name in main_model_names) {

  if (model_name == "Backward AIC") {

    full_fit <- multinom(
      FTR ~ HS + AS + HST + AST + HF + AF +
        HC + AC + HY + AY + HR + AR,
      data = train_main,
      maxit = 500,
      trace = FALSE
    )

    main_fits[[model_name]] <- stepAIC(
      full_fit,
      direction = "backward",
      trace = FALSE
    )

  } else {

    main_fits[[model_name]] <- multinom(
      formulas_main[[model_name]],
      data = train_main,
      maxit = 500,
      trace = FALSE
    )
  }
}
main_fits
```

## 3.3 ANOVA to test whether the statistics add information

First compare the SoT only model with the full model using a likelihood-ratio test. This tests whether the 12 predictors, considered together, improve fit over an SoT only model.

```{r}
anova(main_fits[["Only Shots on target"]], main_fits[["Full statistics"]],test = "Chisq")
```

Adding the remaining statistics to the shots on target model reduced deviance by $2549.75$ and yielded a p-value near 0. This supports rejecting the null hypothesis and using the additional parameters for our end model and that classification is not singularly dominated by the home and away shots on target statistic.

## 3.4 Compare models with AIC

AIC is a useful selection tool, but cannot be relied upon fully to select the 'optimal model'

```{r}
# Compare AIC
main_aic <- data.frame(
  Model = main_model_names,
  AIC = NA_real_
)

for (i in seq_along(main_model_names)) {
  main_aic$AIC[i] <- AIC(main_fits[[main_model_names[i]]])
}

main_aic <- main_aic[order(main_aic$AIC), ]
main_aic
```

The interaction model achieved the lowest AIC ($71848.37$). Backward selection removed "away yellow cards" as a predictor, but only slightly improved AIC over the full model.

# 4. Bookmaker odds

The three models below use only matches with complete values for all 12 match statistics and all three Bet365 opening odds columns.

```{r}
train_odds <- prepare_matches(train_raw, c(stats_all, odds_cols))
test_odds <- prepare_matches(test_raw, c(stats_all, odds_cols))

cat("Training rows in odds comparison:", nrow(train_odds), "\n")
cat("Test rows in odds comparison:", nrow(test_odds), "\n")
```

Missing odds excluded nine additional training matches (approximately $0.024\%$ of the data set) and no test matches. Although the odds training sample is almost identical to the non-odds training set, cross sample AIC comparisons are treated cautiously because the effect of these exclusions has not been looked into.

```{r}
# including bookmaker odds
formulas_odds <- list(

  "Bookmaker odds only" = FTR ~ B365H + B365D + B365A,

  "Statistics plus odds" = FTR ~ HS + AS + HST + AST + HF + AF +
    HC + AC + HY + AY + HR + AR + B365H + B365D + B365A,
  
  "Difference intercation plus odds" = FTR ~ d_sot * t_sot + d_shots +
    t_shots + d_corners + t_corners + B365H + B365D + B365A,

  "Quadratic plus odds" = FTR ~ HST + AST + I(HST^2) + I(AST^2) + HS + AS +
    I(HS^2)   + I(AS^2) + HC + AC + HF + AF + HY + AY + HR + AR + B365H + B365D +B365A
)
# Model names
odds_model_names <- names(formulas_odds)

odds_fits <- list()

# Fit 
for (model_name in odds_model_names) {
  
  odds_fits[[model_name]] <- multinom(
    formulas_odds[[model_name]],
    data = train_odds,
    maxit = 500,
    trace = FALSE
  )
}

# Compare AIC
odds_aic <- data.frame(
  Model = odds_model_names,
  AIC = NA_real_
)

for (i in seq_along(odds_model_names)) {
  odds_aic$AIC[i] <- AIC(odds_fits[[odds_model_names[i]]])
}

odds_aic <- odds_aic[order(odds_aic$AIC), ]
odds_aic
```

# 5. Choosing a model

## 5.1 Select the final model

Our models are compared using AIC. The model with the lowest AIC is selected for further evaluation.

The Premier League test data is not used to select the model yet.

I first explored a difference-total interaction model to capture more complex relationships. However, a closer look showed that with, $d_{sot} = (HST - AST)$ and $t_{sot} = (HST + AST)$ the interaction becomes $d_{sot} * t_{sot} = (HST - AST)(HST + AST) = (HST)^2 - (AST)^2$. Thus, a single interaction coefficient forces home and away squared effects to have equal magnitudes but opposite signs, rather than estimating them independently.

Although this idea took some time to develop and resulted in good performance, it fell short. It instead motivated a more straightforward quadratic model, defined in section 4, that allows for greater flexibility.

```{r}
total_aic <- rbind(main_aic, odds_aic)
total_aic <- total_aic[order(total_aic$AIC), ]
total_aic

selected_model <- total_aic$Model[1]
selected_fit <- total_aic$AIC[1]

cat("Selected model:", selected_model, "\n")
cat("Selected model AIC:", selected_fit, "\n")
```

The quadratic model was preferred by AIC.

## 5.2 Define performance metrics

```{r}
score_predictions <- function(model, test_data) {
  # Predict probs
  probabilities <- predict(model, newdata = test_data, type = "probs")

  # Predict outcome with highest probability
  predicted <- colnames(probabilities)[max.col(probabilities)]
  
  # Percentage correct
  correct_percent <- mean(predicted == test_data$FTR) * 100

  # ROC curves and AUC
  roc_results <- list()
  auc_results <- numeric()

  for (outcome in colnames(probabilities)) {

    roc_results[[outcome]] <- roc(test_data$FTR == outcome, probabilities[, outcome], quiet = TRUE)
    auc_results[outcome] <- as.numeric(auc(roc_results[[outcome]]))
  }
  
  actual_probability <- numeric(nrow(test_data))

  for (i in 1:nrow(test_data)) {
  outcome <- as.character(test_data$FTR[i])
  actual_probability[i] <- probabilities[i, outcome]
  }

  log_loss <- -mean(log(pmax(actual_probability, 1e-15)))

  list(CorrectPercent = correct_percent, LogLoss = log_loss, AUC = auc_results, ROC = roc_results)
}
```

We introduce the log-loss performance measurement as it can be calculated for all models explored by our group, giving us a fair comparison metric.

# 5.3 Training accuracy

```{r}
top_models <- c("Statistics plus odds", "Quadratic plus odds")

training_accuracy <- setNames(numeric(length(top_models)), top_models)

recall <- matrix(nrow = 2, ncol = 3)

for (i in 1:2) {

  fit <- odds_fits[[top_models[i]]]

  training_accuracy[top_models[i]] <- score_predictions(fit, train_odds)$CorrectPercent

  predicted <- predict(fit, newdata = train_odds, type = "class")

  cm_train <- table(
    Actual = factor(train_odds$FTR, levels = outcome_levels),
    Predicted = factor(predicted, levels = outcome_levels)
  )

  print(
    ggplot(as.data.frame(cm_train),
    aes(Predicted, Actual, fill = Freq)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "black") +
    geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightyellow", high = "red") +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(title = paste("Training:", top_models[i]),fill = "Matches") +
    theme_minimal()
     )
  
   recall[i, ] <- 100 * diag(cm_train) / rowSums(cm_train)
}

bars <- barplot(
  recall,
  beside = TRUE,
  names.arg = c("Draw", "Away", "Home"),
  space = c(0.1, 1),
  col = c("steelblue", "red"),
  ylim = c(0, 100),
  ylab = "Correctly predicted (%)",
  main = "Training recall by outcome",
  legend.text = c("Statistics plus odds", "Quadratic plus odds"),
  args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
)

text(bars, recall, labels = paste0(round(recall, 1), "%"), pos = 3, cex = 0.85)

training_table <- data.frame(Accuracy = round(training_accuracy, 2))
training_table
```

# 5.4 10-Fold Cross Validation

```{r}

train_odds$FTR <- factor(train_odds$FTR, levels = outcome_levels)

folds <- createFolds(train_odds$FTR, k = 10, returnTrain = TRUE)

control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, index = folds)

cv_accuracy <- setNames(numeric(length(top_models)), top_models)

for (model_name in top_models) {

  cv_fit <- train(
    formulas_odds[[model_name]],
    data = train_odds,
    method = "multinom",
    trControl = control,
    tuneGrid = data.frame(decay = 0),
    maxit = 500,
    trace = FALSE
  )
  
  cv_accuracy[model_name] <- 100 * cv_fit$results$Accuracy
}

cv_table <- data.frame(CV_accuracy = round(cv_accuracy, 2))
cv_table


```

Cross-validated accuracies of $55.6\%$ and $56.2\%$ closely match training performance, suggesting little over fitting under this validation scheme.

# 6. Premier League test

## 6.1 Compare every main model

Every fitted model is evaluated on the same Premier League test rows.

```{r}
all_fits <- c(main_fits, odds_fits)

all_results <- list()

for (model_name in names(all_fits)) {

  if (model_name %in% names(odds_fits)) {
    all_results[[model_name]] <- score_predictions(all_fits[[model_name]],test_odds     )
  } else {
    all_results[[model_name]] <- score_predictions(all_fits[[model_name]],test_main     )
  }
}

# Create results table
results_table <- data.frame(
  Model = character(),
  AIC = numeric(),
  CorrectPercent = numeric(),
  Logloss = numeric(),
  AUC_Home = numeric(),
  AUC_Draw = numeric(),
  AUC_Away = numeric()
)

# Fill results table
for (model_name in names(all_fits)) {

  results_table[nrow(results_table) + 1, ] <- list(
    model_name,
    AIC(all_fits[[model_name]]),
    all_results[[model_name]]$CorrectPercent,
    all_results[[model_name]]$LogLoss,
    all_results[[model_name]]$AUC["H"],
    all_results[[model_name]]$AUC["D"],
    all_results[[model_name]]$AUC["A"]
  )
}

results_table[, -1] <- round(results_table[, -1], 3)
results_table
```

The full model achieved $57.12\%$ accuracy, compared with $55.98\%$ using the shots on target only model and $51.40\%$ when excluding shots on target from the full model. Shots on target are therefore important, but do not capture all available information which is further backed by our ANOVA test in section 3.3.

Adding bookmaker odds increased the full model’s accuracy to $60.13\%$, slightly exceeding the difference interaction with odds model’s $59.79\%$. Although AIC favoured the interaction model, the full statistics plus odds model achieved higher test accuracy. This highlights that a better penalised training fit does not necessarily manifest into better classification performance.

The quadratic plus odds model achieved the highest overall accuracy of $60.56\%$.

## 6.2 ROC curves

```{r ROC}
top_3 <- c("Statistics plus odds", "Quadratic plus odds", "Full statistics")

model_colours <- c("blue", "red", "darkgreen")

# Plot ROC curves for home wins
plot(
  all_results[[top_3[1]]]$ROC[["H"]],
  col = model_colours[1],
  main = "ROC Curves - Home Wins"
)

for (i in 2:3) {
  plot(
    all_results[[top_3[i]]]$ROC[["H"]],
    col = model_colours[i],
    add = TRUE
  )
}

legend("bottomright", legend = top_3, col = model_colours, lty = 1)


# Plot ROC curves for draws
plot(
  all_results[[top_3[1]]]$ROC[["D"]],
  col = model_colours[1],
  main = "ROC Curves - Draws"
)

for (i in 2:3) {
  plot(
    all_results[[top_3[i]]]$ROC[["D"]],
    col = model_colours[i],
    add = TRUE
  )
}

legend("bottomright", legend = top_3, col = model_colours, lty = 1)


# Plot ROC curves for away wins
plot(
  all_results[[top_3[1]]]$ROC[["A"]],
  col = model_colours[1],
  main = "ROC Curves - Away Wins"
)

for (i in 2:3) {
  plot(
    all_results[[top_3[i]]]$ROC[["A"]],
    col = model_colours[i],
    add = TRUE
  )
}

legend("bottomright", legend = top_3, col = model_colours, lty = 1)

```

The two odds enhanced models have almost identical ROC performance, with AUCs of $0.799-0.807$ for home wins, $0.815-0.823$ for away wins and $0.63-0.67$ for draws. Both outperform the full statistics model across all three outcomes.

Draws remain the hardest outcome to classify, even after introducing odds. One possible reason is that two teams can record similar shots and shots on target, yet one still wins narrowly. This overlap makes it harder for the model to identify a clear pattern separating draws from wins.

## 6.3 Confusion matrix

```{r}
fit <- odds_fits[["Quadratic plus odds"]]

predicted <- predict(fit, newdata = test_odds, type = "class")

cm <- table(
  Actual = test_odds$FTR,
  Predicted = factor(predicted, levels = outcome_levels)
)

ggplot(as.data.frame(cm), aes(Predicted, Actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightyellow", high = "red") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Confusion matrix - Quadratic plus odds", fill = "Matches") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The confusion matrix displays a clear weakness in identifying draws, only $151$ of $2159$ actual draws were correctly classified ($6.99\%$), with most predicted as home wins. Alternatively, the model correctly identified $83.1\%$ of home wins and $70.5\%$ of away wins. We have a strong win classification but a very poor draw classification with this model.

## 6.4 Training and Test accuracy comparison

```{r}

premier_accuracy <- sapply(top_models, function(model_name) {
  all_results[[model_name]]$CorrectPercent
})

accuracy_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = top_models,
  Training = as.numeric(training_accuracy[top_models]),
  Cross_validation = as.numeric(cv_accuracy[top_models]),
  Premier_League = as.numeric(premier_accuracy)
)

accuracy_comparison$CV_minus_Premier <- 
  accuracy_comparison$Cross_validation -  
  accuracy_comparison$Premier_League

accuracy_comparison[, -1] <- round(accuracy_comparison[, -1], 2)
accuracy_comparison
```

Premier League test accuracy exceeded cross-validated lower league training accuracy by $4.5\%$ for the statistics plus odds model and $4.3\%$ for the quadratic plus odds model. This observation is quite strange as accuracy would typically decrease on test data, I suspect this improvement may reflect the Premier League sample’s lower proportion of draws and higher proportion of home wins. We explored the models weakness in predicting draws and higher accuracy for home wins, this leaves less area for the model to struggle, which may in turn produce this observed artificially boosted performance.

# 7. Conclusion & Limitations

## 7.1 Conclusion

The quadratic plus odds model achieved the highest accuracy of $60.56\%$, compared with $45.49\%$ for the majority class baseline discussed in the initial EDA section.

Feature sensitivity analysis helped identify where the information came from. Using backwards AIC for the full model we identified, away yellow cards as the least important predictor. Removing shots on target reduced accuracy from $57.12\%$ to $51.40\%$, while the shots on target only model achieved $55.98\%$. Therefore SoT account for much but not all of the information/model’s performance. Adding bookmaker odds provided further gains to accuracy.

Our key finding was the model’s poor ability to predict draws. The quadratic plus odds model only correctly identified a strikingly low $6.99\%$ of actual draws, compared to a respectable $83.1\%$ of home wins and a moderate $70.5\%$ of away wins.

The confusion matrix changed our interpretation of overall performance. The multinomial model was reasonably effective at identifying wins, but was not a balanced three outcome classifier, especially for draws.

## 7.2 Limits of the data set

The available data limits how accurately we can distinguish draws from narrow victories. Similar numbers of shots, shots on target and corners can accompany either result, leaving no clear statistical separation. Adding more parameters cannot fully compensate for missing information.
